rationale: B wins because it is more ruthless about proof and reporter reality: "Partial disclosure kills this angle" is the sentence that saves a founder from getting carved up by a trade reporter. A has real bones, but "Anker just set the timeline" turns one launch into a category clock without the comparison set it admits it still needs. The difference is not formatting; B knows when the angle is pitchable and when it is still just a tempting thought.
gaps_in_A: "Anker just set the timeline" overclaims the category significance from one company launch.
"The installation barrier has been cited repeatedly as the main friction point" is not in the supplied facts; it needs sourcing or it comes out.
"home battery adoption has been slower than solar's trajectory" is imported context, not grounded in the update.
"value-oriented buyers" invents a buyer psychographic from Anker's charger reputation. Useful hunch, not a fact.
gaps_in_B: "The prevailing belief is that whole-home batteries mean panel work, transfer switches, and an electrician's week" is too specific to smuggle in without evidence.
"purchase costing thousands of dollars and living on the side of the house for a decade" leans on likely category context, but the update withholds pricing and warranty terms.

"A profitable charger maker bets on a capital-heavy market" is distinct, but the set admits it is thin: "should not be pitched until at least one financial detail exists." That belongs closer to watchlist than lead angle.
"service obligations it has never carried at this scale" is plausible, but still an inference. Name it as a question, not a fact.
